title: Berkshire 2010 letter: BNSF, intrinsic value, GEICO goodwill, float, culture, and leverage
summary: Buffett's 2010 letter explains how to judge intrinsic value (investments, operating earnings, and how retained earnings get deployed), why capital-allocation flexibility and an owner-minded culture are Berkshire's edge, and how GEICO's goodwill far exceeds book value. It also covers insurance discipline and float, ignoring net income, and avoiding leverage.

principles.text: Set performance goals up front; otherwise management paints the bull's-eye around wherever the arrow lands.
principles.quote: Lacking such standards, managements are tempted to shoot the arrow of performance and then paint the bull’s-eye around wherever it lands.

principles.text: Value a company on what it has now plus what management will do with retained earnings.
principles.quote: This “what-will-they-do-with-the-money” factor must always be evaluated along with the “what-do-we-have-now” calculation in order for us, or anybody, to arrive at a sensible estimate of a company’s intrinsic value.

principles.text: Insurance discipline includes the willingness to walk away when the right premium can't be obtained.
principles.quote: The willingness to walk away if the appropriate premium can’t be obtained.

principles.text: Flexibility across industries and securities is a capital-allocation edge; when businesses are overpriced, buy securities and wait.
principles.quote: Often, businesses are priced ridiculously high against what can likely be earned from investments in stocks or bonds. At such moments, we buy securities and bide our time.

principles.text: Prefer being approximately right to being precisely wrong; students should learn to value businesses.
principles.quote: We would rather be approximately right than precisely wrong.

principles.text: Avoid leverage and hold ample liquidity so you can play offense when others scramble for survival.
principles.quote: The fundamental principle of auto racing is that to finish first, you must first finish.
